summary: This is a conference abstract submitted to the SFCR 2025 (Société Française de Chirurgie Rachidienne) describing an AI algorithm designed to prioritize patient consultations for lumbar pathology. A neural network model was trained on 3,500 patients with 20 clinical variables and achieved an AUC-ROC of 75.2%, accuracy of 70.3%, and sensitivity of 74.5%. The model is now planned for prospective clinical validation via an online tool.

content_blocks.title: Introduction & Objective
content_blocks.content: The abstract addresses the problem of overcrowded specialist consultations in spinal pathology worldwide, leading to treatment delays for patients and excessive workload for surgeons. The objective was to create a prediction algorithm to identify which patients should be seen as a priority. AI is proposed as a tool to direct patients to the right specialist at the right time and reduce inefficiencies.

content_blocks.title: Material & Methods
content_blocks.content: Dataset: 3,500 patients consulting for lumbar symptoms, each with 20 clinical variables. Label: 16% of patients (n≈560) were operated within one year of first consultation, defining the 'priority' class. Platform: Sciencer platform used to democratize health prediction. Data split into training and test sets. Clinicians contributed clinical expertise to select the best prediction model. Three phases of variable reduction were performed, reducing from 20 to 10 variables. Final model: neural network.

content_blocks.title: Results & Model Performance
content_blocks.content:
After 3 testing phases reducing variables from 20 to 10, a neural network model was selected. Performance metrics:
- AUC-ROC: 75.2% (good discrimination between priority and non-priority patients)
- Accuracy: 70.3%
- Sensitivity: 74.5% (effective identification of priority patients, limiting false negatives)
- F1-score: 45.5% (model tends to over-triage, i.e., overestimates urgent cases — considered beneficial to the patient)
Key variable: Oswestry Disability Index score elevation was strongly associated with probability of needing rapid consultation, supporting clinical relevance.

content_blocks.title: Conclusion & Next Steps
content_blocks.content: Results encourage integration of the model into clinical practice. The model will be validated prospectively via an online tool. Future developments include: integration of imaging data, and extension to cervical pathology. No conflicts of interest declared.

key_findings: Neural network model trained on 3,500 lumbar patients (20 clinical variables) to predict priority consultation need (defined as surgery within 1 year of first visit; 16% prevalence).
Model achieved AUC-ROC of 75.2%, accuracy of 70.3%, sensitivity of 74.5%, and F1-score of 45.5% after reducing variables from 20 to 10.
The model tends to over-triage (overestimate urgency), which is considered acceptable as it benefits the patient.
Oswestry Disability Index score was identified as a key predictor of priority consultation need.
The Sciencer platform was used to integrate data and allow clinicians to select the best predictive model.
Prospective clinical validation via an online tool is planned as the next step.
Extensions to imaging data integration and cervical pathology are in progress.
